notes:
1. Economic Planning in India — Basic Idea

  • Economic planning became a major instrument of India's development strategy after Independence.
  • Five-Year Plans guided resource allocation and national development priorities.
  • Planning aimed at growth, agriculture, industry, infrastructure, employment, poverty reduction and improvement in living standards.
📌 Must-Memorise

India after Independence → Planned Economic Development

2. Planning in India's Mixed Economy

  • India's planning system operated within a mixed economy.
  • Government determined broad development priorities.
  • Public-sector and private-sector enterprises both participated in economic activity.
  • Private property and market activity continued throughout the planning period.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Indian Planning ≠ Complete Command Economy

3. Five-Year Plans — Overall Period

  • India implemented twelve Five-Year Plans.
  • The First Five-Year Plan began in 1951.
  • The Twelfth Five-Year Plan ended in 2017.
  • India did not introduce a Thirteenth Five-Year Plan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Five-Year Plans → 1951–2017

Total → 12 Plans

4. Pre-Independence Planning — Background

  • Ideas of planned economic development existed before Independence.
  • Individuals, political organisations and industrialists proposed different plans.
  • These plans differed in ideology, sectoral priorities and the proposed role of the State.

5. M. Visvesvaraya — Planned Economy for India

  • Sir M. Visvesvaraya published Planned Economy for India in 1934.
  • He advocated rapid industrialisation and economic planning.
  • His approach emphasised raising national income through industrial development.
📌 Must-Memorise

1934 → Planned Economy for India → M. Visvesvaraya

6. National Planning Committee — 1938

  • The Indian National Congress established the National Planning Committee in 1938.
  • Jawaharlal Nehru served as its Chairman.
  • It examined coordinated national development.

Its major concerns included:

  • Industrialisation.
  • Agriculture.
  • Social services.
  • Improvement of living standards.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Planning Committee → 1938 → Jawaharlal Nehru

7. Bombay Plan — Industrialists' Proposal

  • The Bombay Plan was prepared by leading Indian industrialists during the 1940s.
  • It proposed large-scale investment for economic development.
  • Although prepared by industrialists, it accepted an important role for the State.

Important personalities included:

  • J. R. D. Tata.
  • G. D. Birla.
  • Purshottamdas Thakurdas.
  • Kasturbhai Lalbhai.
  • Lala Shri Ram.
  • Ardeshir Dalal.
  • A. D. Shroff.
  • John Mathai.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bombay Plan → Industrialists, Not Government

8. People's Plan — M. N. Roy

  • The People's Plan was associated with M. N. Roy.
  • It placed greater emphasis on agriculture and consumer goods.
  • It also favoured nationalisation of important sectors.
📌 Must-Memorise

People's Plan → M. N. Roy

9. Gandhian Plan — Sriman Narayan Agarwal

  • The Gandhian Plan was associated with Sriman Narayan Agarwal.
  • It reflected Gandhian ideas of decentralised development.

It emphasised:

  • Village development.
  • Agriculture.
  • Cottage industries.
  • Small-scale production.
  • Decentralisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gandhian Plan → Sriman Narayan Agarwal

10. Sarvodaya Plan — Jayaprakash Narayan

  • The Sarvodaya Plan was associated with Jayaprakash Narayan.
  • It drew inspiration from Gandhian economic thought.

It emphasised:

  • Agriculture.
  • Rural development.
  • Decentralisation.
  • Community-based economic organisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sarvodaya Plan → Jayaprakash Narayan

11. Pre-Independence Planning — Key Pairings

  • Visvesvaraya → Planned Economy for India.
  • Jawaharlal Nehru → National Planning Committee.
  • Indian industrialists → Bombay Plan.
  • M. N. Roy → People's Plan.
  • Sriman Narayan Agarwal → Gandhian Plan.
  • Jayaprakash Narayan → Sarvodaya Plan.

12. India After Independence — Economic Problems

India faced:

  • Low agricultural productivity.
  • Food shortages.
  • Limited industrial capacity.
  • Poor infrastructure.
  • Low savings and investment.
  • Widespread poverty.
  • Unemployment.
  • Low literacy.
  • Weak health conditions.

13. Planning Commission — 1950

  • The Planning Commission was established in 1950.
  • It formulated India's Five-Year Plans.
  • It recommended allocation of development resources.
📌 Must-Memorise

Planning Commission → 1950

14. First Five-Year Plan — 1951–1956

  • The First Five-Year Plan operated from 1951 to 1956.
  • It was India's first formal Five-Year Plan.
  • Agriculture received the highest priority.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Plan → 1951–1956 → Agriculture

15. First Plan — Harrod-Domar Model

  • The First Plan was broadly based on the Harrod-Domar growth model.
  • It emphasised the relationship between savings, investment, capital formation and economic growth.

Core logic:

Savings → Investment → Capital Formation → Growth

📌 Must-Memorise

First Plan → Harrod-Domar

16. ICOR — Incremental Capital-Output Ratio

  • ICOR stands for Incremental Capital-Output Ratio.
  • It indicates the additional capital required to produce an additional unit of output.
  • A lower ICOR generally indicates greater capital efficiency.

A simplified growth relationship is:

Growth Rate = Savings Rate ÷ Capital-Output Ratio

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Lower ICOR → Greater Capital Efficiency

17. First Plan — Why Agriculture Received Priority

Important reasons included:

  • Food shortages.
  • Inflation.
  • Refugee rehabilitation.
  • Weak agricultural output.

Major focus areas were:

  • Agriculture.
  • Irrigation.
  • Power.
  • Community development.
  • Transport.
  • Rehabilitation.

18. First Plan — Major Multipurpose Projects

Important early projects included:

  • Bhakra-Nangal Project.
  • Damodar Valley Project.
  • Hirakud Project.

They supported:

  • Irrigation.
  • Electricity generation.
  • Flood control.
  • Regional development.

19. Community Development Programme — 1952

  • The Community Development Programme was launched in 1952.
  • It aimed at coordinated rural development.

It covered:

  • Agriculture.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Local development.
📌 Must-Memorise

Community Development Programme → 1952

20. National Extension Service — 1953

  • The National Extension Service was introduced in 1953.
  • It aimed to extend development activities across rural areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Extension Service → 1953

21. First Plan — Core Memory

First Plan → Harrod-Domar + Agriculture + Irrigation + Rehabilitation

22. Second Five-Year Plan — 1956–1961

  • The Second Plan operated from 1956 to 1961.
  • It marked a major shift towards rapid industrialisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Second Plan → 1956–1961 → Heavy Industry

23. Second Plan — Mahalanobis Model

  • The Second Plan was based primarily on the P. C. Mahalanobis model.
  • Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis played a major role in shaping the strategy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Second Plan → Mahalanobis Model

24. Mahalanobis Model — Heavy Industry Strategy

The model emphasised:

  • Heavy industries.
  • Capital-goods industries.
  • Domestic industrial capacity.
  • Long-term growth.

The strategy expected investment in capital goods to expand India's future ability to produce machinery and industrial equipment.

📌 Must-Memorise

Mahalanobis → Heavy Industry + Capital Goods

25. Capital Goods vs Consumer Goods

Capital goods:

  • Used to produce other goods and services.
  • Examples include machinery and industrial equipment.

Consumer goods:

  • Directly used by consumers.
  • Examples include food, clothing and household goods.

26. Second Plan — Public-Sector Leadership

  • Heavy industrialisation was the central priority.
  • The public sector was expected to lead investment in heavy and basic industries.
  • Large capital requirements and long gestation periods made public investment especially important.

27. Industrial Policy Resolution — 1956

  • The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 strengthened the role of the public sector.
  • It reflected the objective of creating a Socialistic Pattern of Society.
📌 Must-Memorise

Industrial Policy Resolution → 1956

28. Second Plan — Major Steel Plants

  • Bhilai Steel Plant → Soviet Union.
  • Rourkela Steel Plant → West Germany.
  • Durgapur Steel Plant → United Kingdom.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhilai → Soviet

Rourkela → West Germany

Durgapur → United Kingdom

29. First Plan vs Second Plan

  • First Plan → Agriculture.
  • Second Plan → Heavy industry.
  • First Plan → Harrod-Domar.
  • Second Plan → Mahalanobis.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Harrod-Domar → First Plan

Mahalanobis → Second Plan

30. Third Five-Year Plan — 1961–1966

  • The Third Plan operated from 1961 to 1966.
  • Its major objective was to establish a self-reliant and self-generating economy.

Major priorities included:

  • Agriculture.
  • Basic industries.
  • Power.
  • Transport.
  • Education.
  • Self-reliance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Third Plan → Self-Reliance

31. Self-Reliance — Planning Meaning

Self-reliance meant:

  • Building domestic productive capacity.
  • Reducing excessive dependence on imports.
  • Reducing excessive dependence on foreign assistance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Self-Reliance ≠ Complete Isolation

32. Third Plan — Major Disruptions

The Third Plan was affected by:

  • India-China War → 1962.
  • India-Pakistan War → 1965.
  • Severe drought.
  • Food shortages.
  • Resource constraints.
📌 Must-Memorise

1962 → India-China War

1965 → India-Pakistan War

33. Plan Holiday — 1966–1969

  • No regular Five-Year Plan operated between 1966 and 1969.
  • This period is known as the Plan Holiday.

Three Annual Plans covered:

  • 1966–1967.
  • 1967–1968.
  • 1968–1969.
📌 Must-Memorise

Plan Holiday → 1966–1969 → Three Annual Plans

34. Plan Holiday — Causes

Important causes included:

  • Wars.
  • Drought.
  • Food shortages.
  • Inflationary pressures.
  • Resource constraints.

35. Plan Holiday — Agriculture and Green Revolution

  • Agriculture again received high priority.
  • The period coincided with expansion of the Green Revolution.

Major components included:

  • HYV seeds.
  • Irrigation.
  • Chemical fertilisers.
  • Pesticides.
  • Agricultural credit.
  • Improved farming practices.

36. HYV and Green Revolution — Key Facts

  • HYV stands for High-Yielding Variety.
  • HYV seeds were an important component of the Green Revolution.
  • The initial major impact was especially visible in wheat production.
📌 Must-Memorise

HYV → High-Yielding Variety

Green Revolution → Early Major Impact → Wheat

37. Fourth Five-Year Plan — 1969–1974

  • The Fourth Plan operated from 1969 to 1974.
  • It emphasised growth with stability.
  • It also aimed at progressive achievement of self-reliance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fourth Plan → Growth with Stability + Self-Reliance

38. Fourth Plan — Wider Policy Context

  • Growth with stability meant expanding the economy while controlling disturbances such as inflation.
  • Major commercial banks were nationalised in 1969.
  • Population control and family planning received greater attention.
📌 Must-Memorise

1969 → Major Bank Nationalisation

39. Fifth Five-Year Plan — 1974 Onwards

  • The Fifth Plan began in 1974.
  • Its original period extended towards 1979.
  • It was terminated before completion.

Major objectives:

  • Removal of poverty.
  • Self-reliance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fifth Plan → Poverty Removal + Self-Reliance

40. Garibi Hatao — Fifth Plan

  • Garibi Hatao means removal of poverty.
  • It became closely associated with the development strategy of the Fifth Plan period.
📌 Must-Memorise

Garibi Hatao → Fifth Plan

41. Minimum Needs Programme — Fifth Plan

  • Minimum Needs Programme was introduced during the Fifth Plan.
  • It aimed to expand access to essential basic services.

It included:

  • Elementary education.
  • Rural health.
  • Drinking water.
  • Rural roads.
  • Rural electrification.
  • Housing support.
📌 Must-Memorise

Minimum Needs Programme → Fifth Plan

42. Twenty-Point Programme — 1975

  • The Twenty-Point Programme was introduced in 1975.

It covered:

  • Poverty reduction.
  • Land reform.
  • Employment.
  • Essential commodities.
  • Housing.
  • Social development.
📌 Must-Memorise

Twenty-Point Programme → 1975

43. Fifth Plan — Early Termination

  • The Janata Party Government terminated the Fifth Plan in 1978.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fifth Plan → Terminated in 1978

44. Rolling Plan — 1978–1980

  • The Rolling Plan was introduced during the Janata Government period.
  • It operated broadly from 1978 to 1980.

It involved:

  • A plan for the current year.
  • A longer-term plan.
  • Annual review and revision.
  • Addition of another year to the planning horizon.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rolling Plan → Janata Government + Annual Revision

45. Rolling Plan vs Fixed Plan

  • Fixed Five-Year Plan → Objectives fixed for a specified five-year period.
  • Rolling Plan → Objectives and allocations reviewed periodically.
  • Rolling planning therefore offers greater flexibility.

46. Sixth Five-Year Plan — 1980–1985

  • The Sixth Plan operated from 1980 to 1985.

Major priorities included:

  • Poverty reduction.
  • Employment.
  • Technological modernisation.
  • Energy development.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Economic growth.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sixth Plan → Poverty + Employment + Modernisation

47. Sixth Plan — Development Approach

  • The Plan recognised that economic growth alone would not automatically eliminate poverty.
  • Employment became a more direct development objective.
  • Technology and productive efficiency received greater emphasis.
  • Energy supply and power generation were also important priorities.

48. Seventh Five-Year Plan — 1985–1990

  • The Seventh Plan operated from 1985 to 1990.
  • Its major theme was Food, Work and Productivity.

Priorities included:

  • Food production.
  • Employment.
  • Productivity.
  • Modernisation.
  • Social justice.
  • Self-reliance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Seventh Plan → Food + Work + Productivity

49. Seventh Plan — Technology and Productivity

The period saw increasing emphasis on:

  • Telecommunications.
  • Computers.
  • Modern technology.
  • Efficient use of resources.
  • Productivity improvement.

50. Annual Plans — 1990–1992

  • India again used Annual Plans after the Seventh Plan.
  • They covered 1990–1991 and 1991–1992.
  • Political instability and severe macroeconomic problems delayed the Eighth Plan.
📌 Must-Memorise

1990–1992 → Annual Plans

51. Balance of Payments Crisis and Reforms — 1991

  • India faced a major Balance of Payments crisis in 1991.
  • Major economic reforms were initiated in the same year.
  • These reforms changed the policy environment for subsequent Five-Year Plans.
📌 Must-Memorise

1991 → BOP Crisis + Economic Reforms

52. Eighth Five-Year Plan — 1992–1997

  • The Eighth Plan operated from 1992 to 1997.
  • It was the first regular Five-Year Plan after the 1991 economic reforms.

Major priorities included:

  • Human development.
  • Employment.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Modernisation.
  • Economic growth.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eighth Plan → Human Development

53. Eighth Plan — Post-Reform Character

  • Greater attention was given to human resources.
  • Employment creation received importance.
  • Private investment became more important in the post-reform framework.
  • Planning increasingly relied on guidance rather than detailed direct control.

54. Indicative Planning — Post-1991

Indicative planning uses:

  • Broad objectives.
  • Policy signals.
  • Incentives.
  • Infrastructure priorities.
  • Coordination.

Government provides broad direction while private firms make a larger share of production and investment decisions.

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Indicative Planning ≠ Complete Government Control

55. Ninth Five-Year Plan — 1997–2002

  • The Ninth Plan operated from 1997 to 2002.
  • It emphasised growth with social justice and equity.

Major priorities included:

  • Agriculture.
  • Rural development.
  • Poverty reduction.
  • Employment.
  • Social justice.
  • Basic services.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ninth Plan → Growth + Social Justice + Equity

56. Tenth Five-Year Plan — 2002–2007

  • The Tenth Plan operated from 2002 to 2007.
  • It adopted explicit monitorable development targets.

Targets covered:

  • Economic growth.
  • Poverty reduction.
  • Employment.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Gender gaps.
  • Environmental outcomes.

It also emphasised:

  • Governance.
  • Programme implementation.
  • Reduction of regional disparities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tenth Plan → Monitorable Targets

57. Eleventh Five-Year Plan — 2007–2012

  • The Eleventh Plan operated from 2007 to 2012.
  • Its central theme was Faster and More Inclusive Growth.

Major areas included:

  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Employment.
  • Agriculture.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Women and children.
  • Scheduled Castes.
  • Scheduled Tribes.
  • Regional balance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Eleventh Plan → Faster and More Inclusive Growth

58. Inclusive Growth — Meaning

Inclusive growth means economic growth that:

  • Creates opportunities.
  • Enables broad participation.
  • Allows wider sections of society to benefit.

59. Twelfth Five-Year Plan — 2012–2017

  • The Twelfth Plan operated from 2012 to 2017.
  • It was India's last Five-Year Plan.
  • Its theme was Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth.

Major priorities included:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Energy.
  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Skills.
  • Employment.
  • Agriculture.
  • Manufacturing.
  • Environmental sustainability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Twelfth Plan → 2012–2017 → Last Five-Year Plan

60. Sustainable Growth — Twelfth Plan

Sustainable growth emphasised:

  • Environmental protection.
  • Resource efficiency.
  • Energy security.
  • Natural-resource management.
  • Long-term ecological sustainability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Twelfth Plan → Inclusive + Sustainable Growth

61. Planning Commission Replaced — 2015

  • Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.
📌 Must-Memorise

2015 → Planning Commission Replaced by NITI Aayog

62. End of Five-Year Planning — 2017

  • The Twelfth Five-Year Plan ended in 2017.
  • India did not introduce a Thirteenth Five-Year Plan.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Last Plan → Twelfth Plan

No Thirteenth Five-Year Plan

63. Evolution of Planning Priorities

The broad evolution was:

Agriculture

→ Heavy Industry

→ Self-Reliance

→ Poverty Reduction

→ Modernisation

→ Human Development

→ Inclusive Growth

→ Sustainable Growth

64. Early, Later and Post-Reform Planning

Early planning concentrated on:

  • Agriculture.
  • Irrigation.
  • Industrialisation.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Capital formation.

Later plans increasingly emphasised:

  • Poverty reduction.
  • Employment.
  • Productivity.
  • Technology.
  • Modernisation.

Post-1991 planning increasingly emphasised:

  • Human development.
  • Social justice.
  • Governance.
  • Inclusion.
  • Sustainability.

65. Harrod-Domar vs Mahalanobis Models

Harrod-Domar:

  • Savings.
  • Investment.
  • Capital requirements.
  • Economic growth.
  • First Plan.

Mahalanobis:

  • Sectoral allocation of investment.
  • Heavy industry.
  • Capital goods.
  • Long-term industrial capacity.
  • Second Plan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Harrod-Domar → First

Mahalanobis → Second

66. Import Substitution — Planning Strategy

  • Import substitution means producing domestically goods that would otherwise be imported.

Its objectives included:

  • Reducing dependence on foreign goods.
  • Saving foreign exchange.
  • Promoting domestic industry.
  • Building technological capacity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Import Substitution → Replace Imports with Domestic Production

67. Self-Reliance — Recurring Planning Objective

  • Self-reliance appeared repeatedly in Indian planning.
  • It aimed to strengthen domestic productive capability.
  • It did not mean complete withdrawal from world trade.

68. Centralised and Decentralised Planning

Centralised planning:

  • Major decisions are taken at the national level.
  • India's early planning system was relatively centralised.

Decentralised planning:

  • Gives greater responsibility to States, local governments and communities.
  • Recognises regional differences in development needs.

69. District and Local Planning

District-level planning can coordinate local needs relating to:

  • Agriculture.
  • Roads.
  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Water.
  • Local infrastructure.

70. Democratic Planning in India

Indian planning operated alongside:

  • Elections.
  • Parliament.
  • State Legislatures.
  • Federalism.
  • Private property.
  • Market activity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Indian Planning ≠ Soviet-Style Complete Command Planning

71. Physical, Financial, Perspective and Annual Planning

Physical planning:

  • Focuses on physical quantities.
  • Examples: steel output, electricity generation and irrigation capacity.

Financial planning:

  • Focuses on monetary resources.
  • Includes expenditure, investment, savings, taxation and borrowing.

Perspective planning:

  • Focuses on long-term development.

Annual planning:

  • Covers one year.
📌 Must-Memorise

Physical → Quantity

Financial → Money

Perspective → Long Term

Annual → One Year

72. Major Annual-Plan Periods

India relied on Annual Plans during:

  • 1966–1969.
  • 1990–1992.

73. Agriculture Across Five-Year Plans

  • First Plan → Strong agricultural priority.
  • Third Plan → Agricultural self-sufficiency.
  • Plan Holiday → Agriculture + Green Revolution.
  • Ninth Plan → Agriculture + rural development.

Agriculture remained important because it affected:

  • Food security.
  • Employment.
  • Rural income.
  • Industrial raw materials.
  • Inflation.

74. Industrial Development Across Plans

  • Second Plan → Heavy industrialisation.
  • Early plans → Basic industries + capital goods + public enterprises.
  • Later plans → Modernisation + productivity + technology.
  • Post-1991 → Greater competition + private investment.

75. Poverty and Employment Across Plans

  • Fifth Plan → Garibi Hatao.
  • Sixth Plan → Poverty reduction + employment.
  • Seventh Plan → Work + productivity.
  • Eighth and later plans → Employment increasingly linked with human development and inclusion.

76. Human Development, Inclusion and Sustainability

  • Eighth Plan → Human development.
  • Ninth Plan → Social justice and equity.
  • Eleventh Plan → Inclusive growth.
  • Twelfth Plan → Inclusive + sustainable growth.
